verdict.rationale: Both reviews find the same core blockers: the f-string SQL injection, the swallowed audit errors, floor-divided `pages`, unvalidated paging input and an inaccurate bulk-deactivation audit trail. Both reach the right verdict. A applied the patch, ran the tests and checked each finding with concrete probes, and its line numbers are mostly right (search.py:13, audit.py:15-16). B did not run anything, which it states honestly, and most of its line references are badly wrong (search.py:105, audit.py:66-67, api.py:20), so the findings are much harder to act on.

Does not point out that already-inactive users also get audit entries.
Has fewer explicit test-gap items for some edge cases, such as a missing actor or already-inactive ids.
b_issues: Did not apply the patch or run the tests, so no findings are verified, although this is disclosed.
Most line numbers are wrong (search.py:105, audit.py:66-67, api.py:20 and 40, users.py:134), apparently taken from the diff file's own line numbering.
Includes speculative or low-value items, such as handlers missing from a router that does not exist in the repo and an index on audit_log.
Does not mention that the README handler table is now stale and lacks the new handlers.

B also confirms the existing tests pass, backs its findings with concrete probes, notes the README rule violation and the stale README table, and adds a short note on what is good.
